name: Lion’s Mane
summary: Lion's mane (Hericium erinaceus) has limited, mixed human evidence for cognition and mood. Small older trials reported improvements on selected outcomes, but a 2022 study found no cognitive benefit and a 2025 acute crossover trial found no overall cognitive or mood benefit. Results are preparation-specific, samples are small, and current evidence does not establish disease treatment or prevention.
description: Human research on lion's mane is still small and heterogeneous. A 2009 randomized trial in 30 adults with mild cognitive impairment reported better HDS-R scores during 16 weeks of roughly 3 g/day dry powder, while a 2019 randomized trial found improvement on MMSE but not the other cognitive tests reported in its abstract. In younger adults, 10 g/day for four weeks did not improve cognition in a 2022 study, a 2023 pilot found one acute Stroop-speed signal with only a trend toward lower stress after 28 days, and a 2025 acute crossover trial found no significant effect on global cognition or mood. Fruiting-body powder, standardized extracts, food-delivered mushroom material, and proprietary mushroom complexes should not be treated as interchangeable.
safetyNotes: Short-term human trials reviewed here did not establish a major recurring safety signal, but they were small and generally lasted only weeks to a few months. These studies do not establish long-term safety, pregnancy or breastfeeding safety, or clinically important drug-interaction risks across different lion's mane preparations.
contraindications: No source-supported preparation-wide contraindication was established in the reviewed human trials; pregnancy, breastfeeding, and medication-interaction safety remain inadequately studied.
interactions: No clinically validated drug interaction was established in the reviewed human trials; this is an evidence gap, not proof that interactions do not occur.
preparation: Clinical studies used materially different products: dry fruiting-body powder, fruiting-body supplements, food-delivered mushroom material, a proprietary 1.8 g/day mushroom complex, and an acute 3 g 10:1 fruiting-body extract. Do not generalize findings across fruiting body, mycelium, extract ratios, or proprietary blends without product-matched evidence.

sources.title: Improving effects of the mushroom Yamabushitake (Hericium erinaceus) on mild cognitive impairment: a double-blind placebo-controlled clinical trial
sources.note: 30 adults with mild cognitive impairment; approximately 3 g/day dry powder for 16 weeks. Lead author affiliation listed as Mushroom Laboratory, Hokuto Corporation.

sources.title: Reduction of depression and anxiety by 4 weeks Hericium erinaceus intake
sources.note: 30 women assigned to lion's mane or placebo cookies for four weeks; small exploratory mood study.

sources.title: Improvement of cognitive functions by oral intake of Hericium erinaceus
sources.note: 12-week fruiting-body supplement trial; MMSE improved, while Benton visual retention and verbal paired-associate learning did not show the same reported benefit.

sources.title: Four Weeks of Hericium erinaceus Supplementation Does Not Impact Markers of Metabolic Flexibility or Cognition
sources.note: 24 college-age participants; 10 g/day for four weeks; no significant cognition or metabolic-flexibility effects.

sources.title: The Acute and Chronic Effects of Lion's Mane Mushroom Supplementation on Cognitive Function, Stress and Mood in Young Adults: A Double-Blind, Parallel Groups, Pilot Study
sources.note: 41 healthy adults completed the chronic arm at 1.8 g/day for 28 days. Investigational product supplied by Sempera Organics; authors reported no sponsor role in study conduct or publication decision.

sources.title: Acute effects of a standardised extract of Hericium erinaceus (Lion's Mane mushroom) on cognition and mood in healthy younger adults: a double-blind randomised placebo-controlled study
sources.note: 18 healthy adults received an acute 3 g 10:1 fruiting-body extract; no significant global cognition or mood effect, with a pegboard signal on an individual test.

claimMap.claim: Human cognition evidence for lion's mane is limited and mixed: small older randomized trials reported improvements on selected cognitive outcomes, while more recent studies in younger adults found no overall cognitive benefit or only isolated task-specific signals.
claimMap.notes: This synthesis deliberately includes null evidence and avoids treating a positive result on one test as proof of broad cognitive enhancement.

qualifiers.population: Adults ranging from mild cognitive impairment cohorts to healthy young adults
qualifiers.directness: Direct human evidence, but small studies with heterogeneous preparations and endpoints

claimMap.claim: In a 2009 randomized placebo-controlled trial of 30 adults aged 50 to 80 with mild cognitive impairment, approximately 3 g/day of dry lion's mane powder for 16 weeks improved HDS-R cognitive scores versus placebo at weeks 8, 12, and 16, but scores declined after supplementation stopped.
claimMap.notes: The trial is small, population-specific, and the lead author affiliation was the Mushroom Laboratory of Hokuto Corporation, which should temper generalization.

qualifiers.population: 30 Japanese adults aged 50-80 with mild cognitive impairment
qualifiers.dose_or_duration: Four 250 mg tablets containing 96% dry powder three times daily for 16 weeks

claimMap.claim: Recent studies in younger adults do not support a broad cognitive-enhancement claim: 10 g/day for four weeks had no significant cognitive effect in a 2022 study, and an acute 3 g 10:1 fruiting-body extract produced no significant global cognition or mood effect in a 2025 crossover trial, despite improvement on an individual pegboard task.
claimMap.notes: Negative overall outcomes are retained to prevent cherry-picking of isolated positive tests.

qualifiers.direction: Null overall cognitive findings with isolated task-specific signals

claimMap.claim: Mood and stress findings are preliminary: a four-week randomized study in 30 women reported lower CES-D and indefinite-complaint scores, while a 2023 pilot in healthy young adults found faster acute Stroop performance and only a statistical trend toward lower subjective stress after 28 days, alongside null and limited negative findings.
claimMap.notes: These small studies do not establish lion's mane as a treatment for depression, anxiety, or stress disorders.

qualifiers.population: Small female cohort and healthy young adults

claimMap.claim: Lion's mane clinical findings are preparation-specific. Trials have used dry fruiting-body powder, fruiting-body supplements, food-delivered mushroom material, proprietary mushroom complexes, and concentrated fruiting-body extract, so efficacy or dose findings from one preparation should not be generalized to all products.
claimMap.notes: This is a product-directness limitation derived from the materially different interventions used across the human trials.

claimMap.claim: Short-term human safety data are reassuring only in a limited sense: the reviewed trials did not identify a consistent major safety signal, but their small samples, short durations, and heterogeneous products do not establish long-term safety, pregnancy or breastfeeding safety, or clinically important drug-interaction risks.
claimMap.notes: This is an evidence-boundary statement, not a claim that long-term use or medication combinations are unsafe.

claimMap.claim: Potential commercial-context bias should be visible: the lead author of the 2009 mild-cognitive-impairment trial was affiliated with Hokuto Corporation's Mushroom Laboratory, and Sempera Organics supplied the investigational product for the 2023 pilot, although that study reports no sponsor role in design, analysis, interpretation, writing, or publication decisions.
claimMap.notes: Commercial involvement does not invalidate a study, but it is relevant context when evidence is sparse and sample sizes are small.

safety: Short-term trial data are limited; long-term, reproductive, and medication-interaction safety are not established across preparations.
dosage: Study context only: human trials used preparation-specific exposures including approximately 3 g/day dry powder for 16 weeks, 1.8 g/day for 28 days, 10 g/day for four weeks, and an acute 3 g 10:1 fruiting-body extract. These are trial regimens, not a universal recommended dose.
typical_dosage: Study context only: human trials used preparation-specific exposures including approximately 3 g/day dry powder for 16 weeks, 1.8 g/day for 28 days, 10 g/day for four weeks, and an acute 3 g 10:1 fruiting-body extract. These are trial regimens, not a universal recommended dose.
